q: As per the Negotiable Instruments Act, a cheque is a bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker and ______.
explain: A cheque is always drawn on a specified banker and is payable only on demand; these two features separate it from other bills of exchange.

q: The person who writes and signs a cheque, ordering his bank to pay a sum of money, is called the
explain: The drawer is the account holder who draws the cheque. The drawee is his bank and the payee is the person to be paid.

q: In a cheque transaction, the drawee is
options: the drawer’s banker on whom the cheque is drawn
the person to whom the amount is payable
the person who signs and issues the cheque
the person who endorses it to another party
explain: The drawee of a cheque is the drawer’s bank, which is directed to pay. The person to be paid is the payee.

q: A written, signed and unconditional promise by a debtor to pay a certain sum of money to a creditor is called a
explain: A promissory note is an unconditional undertaking by the maker (debtor) to pay. A bill of exchange and a cheque are orders to pay, not promises.

q: Which of the following is a primary function of a bank?
options: Acting as trustee or executor of customers’ property
Keeping customers’ securities in safe custody
Collecting cheques and rent on behalf of customers
explain: Accepting deposits (and lending) are primary functions. The other three are agency or utility services offered to customers.

q: When the signature of the drawer on a cheque is not genuine, the cheque is called a
explain: A cheque bearing a fake signature of the drawer is a forged cheque; crossing, staleness and post-dating relate to other features.

q: A bearer cheque can be transferred from one person to another by
explain: A bearer cheque passes by mere delivery. Endorsement plus delivery is the method for an order cheque.

q: A cheque in which the words ‘or order’ appear after the name of the payee is called a/an
explain: The words ‘or order’ after the payee’s name make it an order cheque, payable to the payee or to the person he orders.

q: Which of the following statements about cheques is correct?
options: A bearer cheque needs the endorsement of each holder
An order cheque passes by mere delivery
No endorsement can make a bearer cheque payable otherwise than to the bearer
A bearer cheque can only be paid into a bank account
explain: A bearer cheque always remains payable to the bearer, whatever endorsement is put on it. Only order cheques need endorsement to transfer.

q: In the case of an order cheque, the drawee banker is bound to pay
options: only the payee or the person ordered by him
any person who holds the cheque
only the drawer of the cheque
explain: An order cheque is payable to the named payee or his order. The banker is discharged by payment in due course to that person.

q: Which of the following cheques can be collected by the payee over the counter of the bank?
explain: An open cheque carries no crossing and can be encashed across the counter. All crossed cheques must be paid through a bank account.

q: If two parallel lines are drawn on the front part of a cheque, it is called a
explain: Two parallel lines on the face make it a crossed cheque, which cannot be encashed in cash across the counter.

q: What is the effect of crossing a cheque?
options: The payee can obtain payment only through a bank account
The payee is compelled to open a new account
The payee must endorse the cheque to the bank
The cheque cannot be issued again by the drawer
explain: A crossed cheque is paid only through a bank, so the payee must have a bank account to collect it. He is not forced to open a fresh one for this purpose.

q: Which kind of cheque is considered safer than the others if it is lost or stolen?
explain: Crossing ensures that money goes only into a bank account, so the receiver can be traced. Open and bearer cheques can be encashed over the counter.

q: A cheque carrying two parallel transverse lines but no banker’s name must be paid only to
explain: This is a general crossing, whose effect is that the paying bank may pay only to a banker and not across the counter.

q: A special crossing on a cheque must contain
explain: In a special crossing the name of a particular banker is written, and the cheque must be paid only to that banker. It may be made only once.

q: Which statement about special crossing is correct?
options: It can be converted into a general crossing
It may be made any number of times
It cannot be converted into a general crossing
It allows payment across the counter
explain: A special crossing is permanent: it cannot be turned into a general crossing, and the cheque is payable only to the named banker.

q: What is the effect of a ‘not negotiable’ crossing on a cheque?
options: It stays transferable, but the transferee’s title is no better than the transferor’s
It can no longer be transferred to anyone
It becomes payable only to the drawer
It becomes payable across the counter
explain: ‘Not negotiable’ does not stop transfer; it only means the new holder gets no better title than the person who passed it on.

q: Which crossing is also called restrictive crossing?
explain: Account payee crossing restricts payment to the named payee’s account, so the cheque does not remain negotiable.

q: After which of the following crossings does a cheque cease to be negotiable?
explain: An ‘account payee’ crossing ends negotiability. A ‘not negotiable’ crossing, despite its name, leaves the cheque transferable.

q: Which of the following is NOT a type of crossing of a cheque?
explain: Staleness relates to the age of a cheque, not to crossing. General, special, not negotiable and account payee are crossing types.

q: The words ‘not negotiable’ on a cheque must be accompanied by
explain: A ‘not negotiable’ crossing is added on top of a general or a special crossing.

q: A cheque that bears a date earlier than the date of its actual issue is called
explain: A backdated cheque is an antedated cheque. It is not invalid, unless it is so old that it has become stale.

q: Which statement about a post-dated cheque is correct?
options: The banker may pay it before the date shown
It is valid, but the banker must not pay it earlier than its date
explain: A post-dated cheque is valid and negotiable. Paying it early goes against the drawer’s mandate, so the bank loses its protection.

q: A cheque presented for payment after three months from the date of issue is called
explain: By banking custom a cheque older than 3 months is stale and is not honoured unless the drawer revalidates it.

q: For how long are cheques, drafts, pay orders and banker’s cheques valid from the date of the instrument?
explain: These instruments are valid for 3 months from their date. After that they become stale and need revalidation.

q: A stale cheque will be honoured by the drawee banker only if
options: the payee requests the bank in writing
it is revalidated by the drawer
explain: Because it is out of date, the bank pays a stale cheque only after the drawer revalidates it.

q: Even after a cheque becomes stale, the drawer or endorser remains liable until the claim is barred by limitation of
explain: A stale cheque does not discharge the drawer; liability ends only when the claim is barred by limitation, which is three years.

q: Payment of any cheque can be stopped when an injunction is imposed by a
explain: A court can impose an injunction against payment of any cheque, in addition to the account holder’s own stop-payment instruction.

q: A bank can stop payment of an account holder’s cheques on hearing the news of his
explain: Death, insanity and bankruptcy of the customer end the bank’s authority to pay his cheques.

q: Who can file a criminal case against the drawer of a dishonoured cheque?
options: The payee or the holder in due course
explain: Both the payee and the holder in due course can proceed against the drawer of a dishonoured cheque; the paying banker cannot.

q: A stop-payment instruction from the cheque’s maker to the bank can be given
options: by a written application or by a telephonic message if the bank accepts it
only through an affidavit before a magistrate
only after the cheque becomes stale
explain: The drawer may instruct the bank in writing, or by telephone if the bank is willing to accept such a message.

q: Under the Cheque Truncation System, processing locations in India are consolidated into grids at Chennai, Mumbai and which other city?
explain: The three CTS grids are Chennai, Mumbai and New Delhi.

q: The term ‘CTS-2010 standard’ refers to
options: benchmark security features and field placement prescribed for cheque forms
the maximum amount payable by a cheque
the number of days a cheque stays valid
the format of a bank’s annual report
explain: CTS-2010 is the collective name for the benchmarks on paper quality, watermark, invisible-ink logo, void pantograph and field placement on cheques.

q: Truncation of cheques means
options: debiting the drawer’s account through the internet
printing the MICR band on a cheque leaf
crossing a cheque with two parallel lines
scanning cheques and sending an electronic image instead of the physical cheque
explain: In truncation the physical cheque is stopped at the collecting bank and its scanned image travels through clearing.

q: Into how many grids are cheque processing locations consolidated under CTS?
explain: Cheque processing is consolidated into three grids: Chennai, Mumbai and New Delhi.

q: Which of the following is one of the security benchmarks of CTS-2010 cheques?
explain: CTS-2010 benchmarks include a watermark, the bank’s logo in invisible ink and a void pantograph, besides standard field placement.
